title: One input, one output
objectives: Decide whether a table or rule describes a function
Use the vertical line test on a graph
Read open and closed dots at a jump

screens.prose: A machine was fed these inputs, and someone wrote down what came out each time.
screens.question: What is the machine's output for input 2?

options.why: 5 is one answer, but the table also shows 2 giving 6. You picked one row and ignored the other.
6 is one answer, but the table also shows 2 giving 5. You picked one row and ignored the other.
You averaged the two outputs. The machine never gave 5.5.

options.text: It cannot be told: 2 gave two outputs

hints.text: Find every row where the input is 2.
Two rows have input 2.
Those rows give 5 and 6, so input 2 has no single output.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read every row with input 2.

explain.text: Input 2 appears twice, with two different outputs. Nobody can say what 2 gives. A machine we can use must give each input one output.

screens.prose: This curve shows a rule: input $x$, output any $y$ whose square is $x$. Move the dashed line with the slider. The labels give the heights where it meets the curve.
screens.question: Move the line to $x = 4$. How many points of the curve does it meet?

hints.text: The curve has a top half and a bottom half.
Look above and below the axis at $x = 4$.
The line meets the curve at $y = 2$ and at $y = -2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the meeting points above and below the axis.

byKey.one: You counted the top half only. The line also crosses the bottom half, at $y = -2$.
byKey.four: You gave the input, 4. Count the points where the line meets the curve.

explain.text: At $x = 4$ the line meets the curve at $y = 2$ and $y = -2$. Both square to 4, so input 4 has two outputs. Only at $x = 0$ does the line meet the curve once.

screens.prose: A rule that gives every input exactly one output is called a **function**. The sideways curve failed at $x = 4$. Now drag the line across $f(x) = x^2 - 4$.
screens.question: Is $f(x) = x^2 - 4$ a function?

options.text: Yes: every vertical line meets it once
No: the output 0 comes from both −2 and 2
options.why: You checked a level line, not a vertical one. Two inputs sharing an output is allowed. The trouble is one input with two outputs.

options.text: No: some of its outputs are negative
options.why: Negative outputs are allowed. What matters is one output for each input.

hints.text: Drag the line across. Does it ever meet the curve twice?
Look at $x = -2$ and $x = 2$: two inputs, one output each.
Every vertical line crosses the curve exactly once, so each input has one output.

feedback.correct: Each vertical line meets the curve once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count meeting points along vertical lines.

byKey.shared: You looked for two inputs with one output. That is fine. A rule fails only when one input has two outputs.

explain.text: Each vertical line meets the parabola once: one output per input. Two inputs may share an output, as −2 and 2 share 0. That is allowed; one input with two outputs is not.

screens.prose: This graph jumps at $x = 2$. A hollow dot is a point left out of the graph; a filled dot is a point on it. The dashed line is $x = 2$.
screens.question: What is $f(2)$?

hints.text: Which dot at $x = 2$ belongs to the graph?
The dot at height 3 is filled.
The filled dot is on the graph, so $f(2) = 3$.

feedback.correct: The filled dot at height 3 gives $f(2) = 3$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Only the filled dot is on the graph.

byKey.hollow: You read the hollow dot. It marks a point left out, so 1 is not an output at 2.
byKey.average: You split the difference. The graph has one point at $x = 2$, the filled one.

explain.text: The hollow dot is left out and the filled dot counts. So $x = 2$ has one output, 3, and the graph is a function. This is the edge case: a jump is fine when each input lands on one dot.

screens.prose: Here is a table of (input, output) pairs. Some rows stop it being a function.
screens.question: Tap the two inputs that clash.

hints.text: Look for an input that appears twice.
Input 2 appears in two rows.
Rows 2 and 4 both have input 2, with outputs 5 and 7.

feedback.correct: Input 2 gives 5 in one row and 7 in another.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find an input with two different outputs.

byKey.same-output: You picked inputs 2 and 3, which share the output 5. Sharing an output is allowed.
byKey.r0c0: Input 1 appears once, with one output.
byKey.r2c0: Input 3 appears once. Its output, 5, may be shared.
byKey.r4c0: Input 4 appears once, with one output.

explain.text: Input 2 gives 5 and 7, so the table is not a function. Inputs 2 and 3 sharing the output 5 is fine. Remove one of the input-2 rows and it becomes a function.

screens.prose: Four shares closed at these prices today. Two rules link the columns: stock to price, and price back to stock.
screens.question: Which rule is a function?

options.text: Input a stock, output its close
Input a close, output the stock
options.why: Input £12.40 points to two stocks, AAA and CCC. That input has two outputs.

options.text: Both of them
options.why: Stock to price works, but price to stock fails: £12.40 gives AAA and CCC.

options.text: Neither of them
options.why: Stock to price works: each stock has one close. Two stocks sharing £12.40 is allowed.

hints.text: Try each rule on £12.40.
AAA and CCC both closed at £12.40.
Each stock has one close, but the close £12.40 belongs to two stocks.

feedback.correct: Each stock has exactly one close.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each direction for an input with two outputs.

explain.text: Each stock has one close, so stock to price is a function. Run it backwards and £12.40 has two answers. Undoing a function only works when no two inputs share an output.

screens.prose: This circle is the graph of $x^2 + y^2 = 9$. It is one equation, and it draws one smooth curve. Drag the line across.
screens.question: Is the circle the graph of a function of $x$?

options.text: Yes: it comes from one equation
options.why: You judged by the equation, not the outputs. At $x = 0$ the circle has $y = 3$ and $y = -3$.

options.text: Yes: each level line meets it at most twice
options.why: You tested with level lines. The test uses vertical lines, and most of them meet the circle twice.

options.text: No: input 0 gives both 3 and −3

hints.text: Drag the line to $x = 0$. Where does it meet the circle?
The circle has a top half and a bottom half.
At $x = 0$: $y^2 = 9$, so $y = 3$ or $y = -3$. One input, two outputs.

feedback.correct: Input 0 has two outputs, so the circle is not a function.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count where a vertical line meets the circle.

byKey.one-eq: You trusted the single equation. One equation can still give an input two outputs: $y^2 = 9$ gives 3 and −3.

explain.text: The line at $x = 0$ meets the circle at $(0, 3)$ and $(0, -3)$. So input 0 has two outputs, and the circle is not a function. Its top half on its own would be one.

screens.prose: Here is the test you used. A rule is a **function** when every input in its domain gives exactly one output. Several inputs may share an output. On a graph: $$\text{every vertical line meets the graph at most once.}$$
screens.question: Which of these graphs is a function of $x$?

options.text: A U-shaped parabola, $y = x^2$
A circle around the origin
options.why: A vertical line through the middle meets a circle twice.

options.text: A parabola on its side, $y^2 = x$
options.why: The line $x = 4$ meets it at $y = 2$ and $y = -2$.

hints.text: Picture a vertical line sweeping across each graph.
Only the U-shape is met once by every vertical line.

feedback.correct: Every vertical line meets $y = x^2$ once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a graph no vertical line meets twice.

explain.text: A vertical line at $x = a$ meets $y = x^2$ once, at $(a, a^2)$. The circle and the sideways parabola both have inputs with two outputs.

screens.prose: A broker's fee: £5.00 for trades up to £1,000.00, £8.00 above that up to £5,000.00, and £12.00 above £5,000.00. The graph shows the fee against trade size.
screens.question: What is the fee on a trade of exactly £5,000.00?

hints.text: At 5 on the trade axis, the filled dot sits on the £8.00 step.
Up to and including £5,000.00 the fee is £8.00.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find which dot at £5,000.00 is filled.

byKey.next: You read the next step up. Its dot at 5 is hollow, so it starts just above £5,000.00.
byKey.average: You split the difference. Each trade size gets one fee, from the filled dot.

explain.text: The filled dot at 5 is on the £8.00 step, and the £12.00 step starts with a hollow dot. Each boundary belongs to one band, so each trade gets one fee. That is what makes the fee a function of trade size.

ideas: A function gives every input in its domain exactly one output.
Several inputs may share an output; one input with two outputs breaks the rule.
On a graph, every vertical line must meet the graph at most once.

formula.name: Vertical line test
formula.note: A circle fails: $x = 0$ meets $x^2 + y^2 = 9$ at 3 and −3.

summary.trap: One smooth curve from one equation can still fail: a circle is not a function of $x$.

quiz.prose: A rule gives these (input, output) pairs: $(1, 2)$, $(2, 4)$, $(3, 2)$ and $(4, 8)$.
quiz.question: Is it a function?

options.text: Yes
No: the output 2 appears twice
options.why: Two inputs sharing the output 2 is allowed. Each input still has one output.

options.text: No: the outputs follow no pattern
options.why: A function needs no pattern, only one output per input.

feedback.correct: Each input, 1 to 4, has one output.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether any input has two outputs.

explain.text: Inputs 1, 2, 3 and 4 each appear once. Inputs 1 and 3 share the output 2, which is fine. So the rule is a function.

quiz.prose: A rule: input a positive number, output a number whose square is the input.
quiz.question: Is this rule a function?

options.text: No: input 4 gives both 2 and −2
Yes: input 4 gives 2
options.why: You kept only the positive answer. $(-2)^2$ is also 4, and the rule allows it.

options.text: Yes: every input is positive
options.why: Positive inputs are allowed. The trouble is that each one has two outputs.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for every number whose square is 4.

explain.text: Both 2 and −2 square to 4, so input 4 has two outputs. The rule is not a function. Saying "the positive one" would fix it.

quiz.prose: A fee schedule says: £5.00 for trades of £1,000.00 or less, and £8.00 for trades of £1,000.00 or more.
quiz.question: Is the fee a function of trade size?

options.text: No: a trade of £1,000.00 gets two fees
Yes: each band has one fee
options.why: You checked trades away from £1,000.00. At exactly £1,000.00 both bands apply, giving £5.00 and £8.00.

options.text: Yes: the broker would charge the lower fee
options.why: The schedule does not say which. A rule that needs a guess is not a function.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test a trade of exactly £1,000.00.

explain.text: "Or less" and "or more" both include £1,000.00, so that trade has two fees. Changing one band to "less than" would fix it.

quiz.prose: Three graphs are drawn on the plane.
quiz.question: Which one is the graph of a function of $x$?

options.text: The line $y = 4$
The line $x = 4$
options.why: That line is vertical: input 4 has every output, and other inputs have none.

options.text: The circle $x^2 + y^2 = 4$
options.why: At $x = 0$ the circle has $y = 2$ and $y = -2$.

feedback.correct: $y = 4$ gives every input the one output 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run the vertical line test on each.

explain.text: Every vertical line meets $y = 4$ once, so it is a function: a constant one. The line $x = 4$ is itself vertical, so it fails the test completely.
